questions.questionHtml:
The ideal CPI that we can expect in a pipelined implementation is only 1.1. If we want to further reduce CPI, we need to explore the option of issuing and completing multiple instructions every clock cycle. For example, if we issue and complete two instructions every clock cycle, ideally we should get a CPI of 0.5.0.5. Such processors are called multiple issue processors. So, in multiple issue processors, we Fetch (and execute) more than one instructions at one time (expand every pipeline stage to accommodate multiple instructions).


A single issue processor is basically “one instruction each clock cycle” processor.

A computer can parallelize the program execution by using multiple issue processor.

Assume that a program execution takes 100100 nsec when executed on a single issue processor and it takes 4040 nsec when it is executed on a 44-issue processor(i.e. Four instructions each clock cycle). Assuming that some part of the execution is non-parallelizable(i.e. will not benefit from multiple issue processing) then what percentage of execution is non parallelizable ? (Rounded off to nearest integer)

Consider the following instruction sequence in a single-issue in-order 55-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, and WB).  Opcode  Destination  Source1  Source2  ADD R1R2R3 (First instruction to enter the pipeline)  SUB R2R3R1 MUL R1R2R3 ( Last instruction to enter the pipeline)  Opcode  Destination  Source1  Source2  ADD R1R2R3 (First instruction to enter the pipeline)  SUB R2R3R1 MUL R1R2R3 ( Last instruction to enter the pipeline)  How many data hazards does the ID stage need to detect for this instruction sequence?

Consider an unpipelined processor. Assume that it has 11-ns clock cycle and that it uses 44 cycles for ALU operations and 55 cycles for branches and 44 cycles for memory operations. Assume that the relative frequencies of these operations are 50%,35%50%,35% and 15%15% respectively. Suppose that due to clock skew and set up, pipelining the processor adds 0.150.15 ns of overhead to the clock. Ignoring any latency impact, how much speed up in the instruction execution rate will we gain from a pipeline?
